<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with a genuinely narrow, well-tracked clash. CON built a memorable frame ("repair the thermometer, don't hand it to the person it judges") and a strong dilemma: either the worker decides (exit on demand) or the platform decides (nothing changes). PRO neutralized that dilemma with clean symmetry — CON's own remedies (fraud filtering, appeals, human review) all require an adjudicator, so discretion is fatal to both mechanisms or neither — and then specified the real difference: under the motion the score ceases to be sufficient grounds once abuse is credibly raised, with the burden on the platform. That is a substantive change in entitlement, and it fits the motion's own wording ("should be able to," "strongly shaped by"), which undercuts CON's repeated insistence that the motion grants unconditional exit. CON's closing textualist gambit ("judge the words on the page") therefore rested on a reading PRO had already shown to be less faithful than its own. PRO's averaging argument (large samples stabilise systematic bias rather than dilute it) was the sharpest technical hit of the debate and was only partially answered by CON's "bias runs through alternatives too." CON's strongest live route — the two-tier market where the worst workers become least visible — was materially damaged when CON, under PRO's pressure question, enumerated telemetry, route data, safety-carved completion rates and substantiated complaints, letting PRO reply that those are precisely its own alternatives and nobody becomes invisible. CON's "shrinkage" narrative was well executed and kept the debate close, but PRO's "who owns the outcome — a right or a favour that vanishes at 1 a.m." answered it in principle rather than dodging it. Both sides answered pressure questions with proper A1:/A2: labels; both leaned on one phantom reference id, which cancels out.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Pressure Question demanding CON name a metric by which a groped driver who ends a ride can be judged without penalty. CON's answer (telemetry, safety-carved completion, substantiated complaints, cleaned record) both conceded that raw customer sentiment cannot ground deactivation and handed PRO the reply that CON's replacement metrics are PRO's alternatives — collapsing CON's two-tier-market harm while PRO's entitlement-versus-discretion distinction survived.</best_rebuttal>
